2: Pool training for racehorses is said to have begun in 1950s America. It slims a horse down without stressing the legs and refreshes it. Making the horse rely on people in the water is also a way to bond with horses that have temperament issues.
5: A treadmill belt is set inside a deep horse pool so the horse stands in water up to its shoulders. Buoyancy takes about 40% off its weight, while the water adds resistance, so it is often used for rehab after injury layoffs.
8: Before modern medicine, all sorts of recovery methods were tried on racehorses. One trainer was devoted to chiropractic care; legend says it saved a poisoned horse's life and restored the breeding ability of imported sire Saint Crespin.
11: The Thoroughbred, said to be the world's most expensive animal, gets the latest medical care. Heat therapy and shockwave treatment are now common, with know-how building up both on the ground and in research.
14: No horse can race until it passes the gate test. Young horses first practise walking through and standing in a gate with both doors open. Breaking well and getting up to speed means a pass; good gate results show a strong stable.
17: Gate skill varies a lot, and horses like Rulership got slower to break with age. A common drill ties the horse in the gate to sharpen its focus so it jumps out quickly. But a horse that does it in training won't always do it on race day.
20: Horses once wore two kinds of shoes: tough iron 'training shoes' for work and light aluminium 'race shoes' for racing. Swapping to race shoes on race-day mornings made race days famously hard work for farriers.
23: Five-time champion Shinzan had such a huge stride that his hind hooves struck his forelegs and bled. The fix was the 'Shinzan shoe': slipper-like hind covers and T-shaped front bridges, more than twice the weight of normal shoes.
26: The old Shirai annex before Miho had only small tracks, so the usual 2000m+ long works were impossible. The makeshift answer was a fast work over about 5 furlongs (1000m). It worked so well that it is still the standard today.
29: Next to the slope, the woodchip course is the most popular at the training centers. The fine wood chips cushion the legs, but give little rebound, so horses must work harder to run, building the muscles around the legs efficiently.
32: When a horse stops improving, trainers sometimes add jumping work, starting with stepping over poles on the ground or hopping low brush fences. Jumping builds confidence, lifts the horse's mood and works muscles it rarely uses.
35: Real jump schooling also teaches a horse to use its hindquarters powerfully. In Europe jumps racing is its own world with specialist sires, but in Japan sons of stayers often shine over jumps, like Stay Gold's son Oju Chosan.
38: Turf courses are used for training less than you might think. Horses run fast and easily there, which is hard on the legs, yet the springy ground makes it hard to load them. It is mostly used to give lazy work horses a feel for race pace.
41: On work days, hundreds of horses breeze within hours, and when, where and how is the trainer's craft. Once, G1 winner Zenno Rob Roy appeared on the turf, dodging the busy courses to run long and steady and trim down his body.
44: Horses are said to like steady, continuous sounds. Playing soft classical music in the stalls caught on from the Showa to Heisei eras, to help horses switch on and focus in races. Farms and training centers use it widely too.
47: Horses are grazing animals, timid and sensitive. Roaring crowds can panic them so they can't show their true ability. To counter this, stables often blast loud pop songs in the stalls so horses learn not to flinch at noise.
50: The slope, an uphill training course, was built when the training centers opened. It loads a horse efficiently without a flat-out gallop. The trainer who first saw its value was truly ahead of his time: 'build the strongest horse by training'.
53: Unbeaten two-time Classic winner Mihono Bourbon was forged on the Ritto slope. His sprint pedigree always raised doubts about distance, but Spartan slope work gave him the stamina to come within a step of the Triple Crown.
56: While the norm was hard work in small groups, one trainer sent out five or more horses together for light exercise, teaching them to settle and move in a group. Modelled on horse-first racing abroad, it shook Japan and became a major trend.
59: 'Horses are herd animals.' Believing this, a trainer rode many horses together in long, patient sessions. Young horses copied the veterans and learned to use their bodies, and the whole stable became an elite group.
62: Shying at new things is called 'monomi'. To prevent it, horses visit the course during race week: this is schooling. Oguri Cap trained at Nakayama before his first Arima Kinen, partly to slim down. He only dropped 2kg, but he won.
65: El Condor Pasa reshaped his action for Europe over a long stay in France, and Loves Only You went to the track with a lead pony and won at the Breeders' Cup alongside Marche Lorraine. Abroad, adapting to local conditions decides results.
68: Hay and carrots, but also apples, bananas and sugar cubes: food matters to equine athletes, and each stable has its tricks. Nice Nature's groom is said to have mixed pricey viper powder, bought with his own money, into his feed before races.
71: Some stables have a 'Feed Man' who manages feed for every horse, mixing oats, hay and pellets in the right balance for each one's condition and race plan. For horses under heavy stable stress, he is key to keeping them in top shape.
74: Training centers often have forest-lined paths, such as the route to the slope. Walking there helps horses relax amid hard training. Valuing flatwork like walking to the track, not just galloping, is another recent trend.
77: The forest track has gentle, natural slopes, and one stable began using them for long sessions. As more horses joined, hill work was limited to set morning hours. One horse built there was future Derby winner Logi Universe.
80: The slope is used for many kinds of work: everyday canters, medium '15-15' work and hard paired works close to racing. One stable runs six or seven horses in single file to teach race pace and get them used to kickback.
83: A method from a famous stable known for star sprinters. In race week the string goes up the slope and each horse sprints in turn: held early, then flat out over the last 2 furlongs to the end. That contrast built a sprint dynasty.
86: A jockey known for fine horsemanship spent hours with young horses in a small 'arena' at a local track. No speed, just small cues and responses, believing that dialogue would pay off in races. The pair later won a graded race.
89: Dressage was once seen as a world apart from racing, but its aim, a horse easy for its rider to control, was adopted with its methods. Derby winners Eishin Flash and Shahryar, for a trainer who rode at university, embody it.
92: The hoof is called a horse's 'second heart', and hoof care affects racing. Many greats had hoof trouble. Taiki Shuttle cracked a hoof before going abroad, but recovered with 'four-point' shoeing, using few nails to keep its shape.
95: Deep Impact had thin hooves, so his shoes were glued on with a putty-like material instead of nailed, easing the strain. It began as a filler for damaged hooves and was repurposed as shoe adhesive; it is now often called 'Equilox'.
98: The New Polytrack course, made of materials like polyester fabric, arrived in the 2000s. It is gentle on legs and fast, so good for building cardio, and barely affected by season or weather. Many stables adopted it at first.
101: Polytrack, which loads horses lightly, is used less these days. Yet one elite Ritto stable still uses it for race-week G1 finishes: hard work until a week before, then a light final breeze that doesn't upset the horse. Range like that makes a top stable.
104: Day and night turnout keeps horses out in the paddock around the clock. The main aim is more exercise, but nights out also help them mature mentally. It also cuts bedding and staff costs, so it has become common in recent years.
107: A GPS logger fitted to the halter now records a horse's movement in the paddock. Besides checking it gets enough exercise, distance and speed data can show spots where horses linger, helping farms improve their paddocks.
110: 'Slope work' covers many kinds of training, including slope work for yearlings. It loads the hind legs efficiently, and is also good for teaching a running posture with the head low and the body stretched out.
113: Yearlings vary hugely in development. On the slope from autumn into winter, many can't yet run straight while others climb at about 14 seconds a furlong. Raising such a wide range together takes skill backed by experience.
116: Some training is done on rough ground, like paddock grass, instead of groomed tracks. Balancing on uneven footing builds core muscles and teaches the horse to carry itself (self-carriage). It is more common in the USA.
119: Building the core and self-carriage on rough ground leads to an ideal running form. American farms put form before the clock; fixing form early, as yearlings, makes training after joining a stable far more effective.
122: Foals are weaned at about six months. Lead horses are adults that live in the paddock with the anxious weanlings, giving them emotional support and exercising with them to help them grow. They really are the foals' teachers.
125: Lead horses have many roles. Besides paddock work, some lead horses guide the horses in training so sessions run smoothly, acting as the leader of the string. Unlike paddock lead horses, these are often young horses.
128: The most basic formation work is running in single file. Following the horse ahead trains them to run straight, gets them used to kicked-up dirt, and teaches them to settle behind others: preparation for real racing.
131: Group work uses many formations and goals: riding slowly two abreast to get used to running in a pack, or close up behind others to build forward drive. Switching between them by day or by growth prepares horses for their first race.
134: Gate schooling for foals aims to remove fear of the gate. A gate is left where they can see it, they stand in a wide gate while led, then with the front doors open... step by step, until they can stand calmly in a closed gate.
137: Standing calmly in a closed gate isn't enough to pass the gate test. The last piece is the start: jumping out as soon as the doors open on the rider's cue. Learning gate skills while young makes for a smooth debut.
140: Horses have four basic gaits: walk, trot, canter and gallop. Hacking is cantering at an easy pace, and teaching a horse to hack under a rider is the first stage of training it to run fast.
143: Like athletes in many sports, horses do base training through mileage. Long runs at a slow pace build basic fitness or serve as a warm-up. The load is light and the risk of injury is low.
146: Many yearlings aren't fully developed, and forcing work leads to injury. Instead of riding nonstop, the staff give proper rest, such as spells of light walker work only, judging each horse's condition. It tests their skill.
149: Daily brushing and trimming of yearlings matters. It's not just for looks: it lowers the risk of skin disease and the massage boosts circulation. It also gets a naturally timid animal used to being handled.
152: Like people, horses can get many illnesses. A classic one that hurts racing is roaring, where a narrowed airway makes a wheezing noise. Satsuki Sho winner Daiwa Major had it, but beat it with surgery and won four G1s.
155: In Britain, home of modern racing, training applies load slowly over a long time. It suits unfinished youngsters and older horses after the long winter, building them up without injury. This careful, horse-first way builds the depth for tough races.
158: In America, stalls at the track are lent to trainers, so horses train on the race course itself. With the same conditions as race day, fitness shows directly in times, and trainers chase set splits. Speed-first training shapes fast US racing.
161: In paired works at the training centers, the outside horse usually leads and the inner horse moves up alongside. Race-like running builds fighting spirit for a late finish, and lets the trainer compare the pair and check each one easily.
164: A great Irish stable now does single-file work on the gallops too, keeping the routine even abroad, with meaning in the order of the five-plus horse 'train'. A top Japanese trainer who raced against them soon tried it at home.
167: The training grounds at Chantilly in France are vast, about 85 Tokyo Domes. There are turf gallops on natural hills and a 4km dirt slope. With few rules and a give-and-take spirit, even fiery horses from abroad settle there.
170: Hong Kong's Conghua training center, opened in 2018, has a rare turf slope. It is gentle and some doubt its load, but it draws attention. Japan now has big woodchip and felt-mixed dirt slopes, as surfaces keep improving.
173: From the Godolphin Arabian, a founding sire of the breed, to Hungary's Kincsem and Northern Taste, stories of great horses and cats go way back. Cats were kept to catch stable mice, and both animals love rubbing against each other.
176: Horses can befriend many animals, even ducks and crows. Some studies say dogs and horses mimic each other's faces while playing. Maybe the many faces horses pull in the stable are them copying the people who care for them.
179: Legendary horses stood out in training too. Ribot, unbeaten in 16 starts, was called 'Il Piccolo' (the little one), yet breeder Federico Tesio sensed rare talent in his work. Tesio died before Ribot debuted, but the wizard was proved right.
182: Legends stood out in training too. US hero Man o' War sharpened up racing a stablemate worth three times his price. Fiery, he once threw his rider over 10m and ran loose on the gallops for 15 minutes. Another 'Big Red' legend.
